blocks.text:
Design the core of a social networking service (Twitter/Instagram-style) built on a directed follow graph: any user can follow another without needing approval, unless the target has blocked them. Blocking a user immediately severs any existing follow relationship between the pair in either direction. A user's feed aggregates posts from everyone they follow, ranked not by raw recency but by an engagement-weighted score that decays over time, so a highly-engaged older post can still outrank a barely-engaged newer one.

  • Actors: User (follows, unfollows, blocks, posts, views a feed), SocialNetworkService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: a directed follow/block graph, post authoring, and engagement-weighted feed ranking.

This differs from the LinkedIn design (symmetric connections requiring mutual acceptance, pure-recency feed ranking) by using an asymmetric one-way follow model with no approval step, a block mechanic that actively tears down existing edges, and a feed score that blends engagement with time decay instead of sorting by timestamp alone.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Follow: a user follows another directly, with no approval required, unless the target has blocked them.
Unfollow: a user removes an existing follow relationship.
Block: a user blocks another; this immediately removes any existing follow between the pair in either direction and prevents the blocked user from following them again.
Posting: a user authors posts, each accumulating likes and comments over time.
Feed generation: aggregate posts from everyone a user follows, ranked by an engagement-weighted, time-decayed score.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many users, follows, and posts must not require touching existing follow logic.
Extensibility: a different scoring formula should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: scoring, notification, and post creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: feed generation is bounded by the number of accounts followed and their post counts.
Thread safety: a follow and a block on the same pair submitted concurrently must resolve to a single consistent outcome.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Does following require approval (like LinkedIn connections), or is it always immediate (like Twitter follows)?
Should blocking also hide the blocked user's past interactions (likes, comments) on the blocker's posts, or only affect the follow graph?
Is engagement limited to likes and comments, or should shares/reposts factor into the score as well?
Should the feed include reposts from followed accounts, or only their original posts?
Should a blocked user be prevented from viewing the blocker's public posts entirely, or only from following them?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Following is a directed, one-way relationship requiring no approval, unlike a mutual-acceptance connection model.
Blocking is a one-way action that actively tears down any existing follow edge between the pair, in either direction, at the moment the block is applied.
Engagement score considers only likes and comments (comments weighted twice as heavily as likes); reposts and shares are noted as a future extension.
Time decay is modeled as a simple inverse-linear function of elapsed time for clarity; a production system would likely tune a more sophisticated decay curve.

blocks.text: The design centers on two core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: User (with following and blocked sets) and Post

items: User: a member with a set of accounts they follow and a set of accounts they have blocked.
Post: content authored by a user, carrying a timestamp, a like count, and a comment count.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A user follows many users and blocks many users, both directed; a user authors many posts

items: User to User (follows) is many-to-many and directed (asymmetric).
User to User (blocks) is many-to-many and directed.
User to Post is one-to-many.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep scoring, notification, and post creation decoupled from the core service.

Why needed: how a post is scored for feed ranking (engagement-weighted with decay today, perhaps machine-learning-driven relevance tomorrow) is a policy decision that changes independently of how follows and posts are stored.

Why it is the best fit: a new scoring formula is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to SocialNetworkService. What it solves: it isolates a frequently-tuned ranking algorithm from stable orchestration logic.
Why needed: follows, rejections, unfollows, and blocks are all events a real social platform would want to react to (push notifications, analytics).

metadata.alt: SocialObserver interface notified by SocialNetworkService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: SocialNetworkService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core follow/block workflow from side effects.
Why needed: post id generation should not be scattered across calling code.
Why it is the best fit: every post is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: User: attributes userId, name, following, blockedUsers; responsibility: represent a member and their own relationship sets.
Post: attributes postId, authorId, content, timestamp, likeCount, commentCount; responsibility: represent one piece of authored content and its engagement.
PostFactory: method createPost(authorId, content, timestamp); responsibility: generate sequential post ids.
SocialNetworkService: the orchestrator; responsibility: manage follow and block state, score and rank feeds, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: PostScoringStrategy and SocialObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: PostScoringStrategy: score(post, currentTime): returns a numeric ranking score for one post at a given point in time.
SocialObserver: onUserFollowed / onFollowRejected / onUserUnfollowed / onUserBlocked: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a successful follow, a block that severs an existing follow, and an engagement-weighted feed ranking.

metadata.alt: Alice follows Bob, who has not blocked her
Carol blocks Alice, which removes Alice's existing follow of Carol as a side effect
An older, high-engagement post outranks a newer, low-engagement one

blocks.text: The end-to-end workflows, alongside their rejection branches, look like this:

metadata.alt: Follow with block check, block with edge removal, feed generation with scoring

items: Follow path: follow → not blocked and not already following → directed edge added.
Follow rejection paths: follow → target has blocked the requester → rejected, or → already following → rejected.
Block path: block → add to blocked set → remove any existing follow edge between the pair in either direction.
Feed path: generate feed → gather posts from everyone followed → score each by engagement with time decay → sort descending.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: follow(followerId, followeeId): adds a directed follow edge, or throws if blocked or already following.
unfollow(followerId, followeeId): removes an existing follow edge.
blockUser(blockerId, blockedId): adds to the blocker's blocked set and removes any existing follow between the pair.
generateFeed(userId, currentTime): returns posts from followed accounts, ranked by the configured scoring strategy.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: FollowNotAllowedException: the target user has blocked the requester.
AlreadyFollowingException: the requester already follows the target.
InvalidUserException: an unknown user id passed to any operation.

blocks.text: The critical race is a follow and a block on the same pair of users submitted at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: A follow and a block on the same pair racing; synchronization ensures a consistent final outcome, never a blocked user left following

blocks.text: Synchronizing both operations on the target user's record ensures the follow-check and the block-and-remove step each happen atomically, so the system never ends up in a state where a blocked user is still following the blocker.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new scoring formula (machine-learning relevance, shares-weighted) is a new PostScoringStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (push, email digest) is a new SocialObserver implementation.
Adding reposts to the feed candidate set is a small change to what generateFeed gathers, not a structural change.
Mutual friend suggestions can reuse the follow graph in a manner similar to LinkedIn's BFS-based degree calculation.
Single Responsibility: User tracks its own relationship sets, PostScoringStrategy computes scores, SocialObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new scoring or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to SocialNetworkService.
Liskov Substitution: any PostScoringStrategy or SocialObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: SocialObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: SocialNetworkService depends on the PostScoringStrategy and SocialObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
Blocking a user who was never following you is a no-op on the follow graph, just adds to the blocked set.
A user attempting to follow themselves should be rejected, even though nothing in the block check would otherwise catch it.
generateFeed for a user following zero accounts returns an empty list, not an error.
A post with zero likes and zero comments still receives a positive-but-low score from time decay alone if the decay function does not floor at zero.
follow / unfollow / blockUser: O(1) average-case set operations.
generateFeed: O(following count times their average post count) to gather candidates, plus O(n log n) to sort by score.
Space: O(users plus follow edges plus posts) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: User, Follow, Block, Post

items: Follow and Block are both directed join tables on User, distinct from each other.
An index on Post(authorId, timestamp) speeds up gathering candidate posts for a feed.
Add reposts and shares as additional engagement signals in the scoring formula.
Support hiding a blocked user's ability to view the blocker's public posts entirely, not just their ability to follow.
Precompute and incrementally update feed scores rather than recomputing on every read.

In a distributed deployment, fan out new posts to followers' feed caches at write time (fan-out-on-write) for very high-follower accounts, rather than computing feeds live at read time for every request.

blocks.text: SocialNetworkService, including follow, unfollow, block, and feed generation:

codes.python:
# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class FollowNotAllowedException(Exception): pass
class AlreadyFollowingException(Exception): pass
class InvalidUserException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class SocialNetworkService:
    def __init__(self, scoring_strategy):
        self.users = {}             # userId -> User
        self.posts = {}             # authorId -> their posts
        self.scoring_strategy = scoring_strategy  # pluggable ranking policy
        self.observers = []          # listeners

    def add_user(self, user):
        self.users[user.user_id] = user  # register a user
        self.posts[user.user_id] = []      # init their post list

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def add_post(self, post):
        self.posts[post.author_id].append(post)  # record a post

    def follow(self, follower_id, followee_id):
        followee = self.users[followee_id]  # look up target
        if follower_id in followee.blocked_users:  # target has blocked the requester
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_follow_rejected(follower_id, followee_id, "Blocked by target user")  # notify
            raise FollowNotAllowedException(f"{followee_id} has blocked {follower_id}")
        follower = self.users[follower_id]  # look up requester
        if followee_id in follower.following:  # already following
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_follow_rejected(follower_id, followee_id, "Already following")  # notify
            raise AlreadyFollowingException(f"{follower_id} already follows {followee_id}")
        follower.following.add(followee_id)  # add the directed edge
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_user_followed(follower_id, followee_id)  # notify

    def unfollow(self, follower_id, followee_id):
        self.users[follower_id].following.discard(followee_id)  # drop the edge if present
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_user_unfollowed(follower_id, followee_id)  # notify

    def block_user(self, blocker_id, blocked_id):
        self.users[blocker_id].blocked_users.add(blocked_id)         # record the block
        self.users[blocked_id].following.discard(blocker_id)           # blocked user no longer follows the blocker
        self.users[blocker_id].following.discard(blocked_id)             # blocker no longer follows the blocked user either
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_user_blocked(blocker_id, blocked_id)  # notify

    def generate_feed(self, user_id, current_time):
        candidates = []  # gathered posts
        for followed_id in self.users[user_id].following:  # scan every followed account
            candidates.extend(self.posts[followed_id])          # include all their posts
        candidates.sort(key=lambda post: self.scoring_strategy.score(post, current_time), reverse=True)  # sort descending by score
        return candidates  # ranked feed

items: Why does blocking remove the follow edge in both directions, even though a block is a one-way action? Because a block is meant to sever the relationship entirely: the blocked user should not see the blocker's content as a follower, and the blocker should not see the blocked user's content either.

Why weight comments twice as heavily as likes in the scoring formula? Comments represent a higher-effort form of engagement than a single tap, a common signal-weighting choice in real feed ranking systems.

How would you extend this to a mutual-friends-style feature? Reuse the follow graph with a set intersection between two users' following sets, similar in spirit to LinkedIn's BFS-based degree calculation but simpler since it only needs direct neighbors.

Asymmetric follow with no approval vs symmetric connection requiring acceptance: asymmetric follow matches how broadcast-style platforms actually work and is simpler to implement, at the cost of not guaranteeing every relationship is mutually consented to (addressed instead via blocking).

Engagement-decay scoring vs pure recency: engagement-decay surfaces more relevant content but is harder to reason about and tune than a simple chronological feed, and can create filter-bubble effects if over-weighted toward engagement.

Fan-out-on-read (compute feed live) vs fan-out-on-write (precompute on post): this design computes the feed live for simplicity; a production system with high-follower accounts would need to fan out new posts to follower feed caches at write time to keep read latency low.
Persist users, follow edges, block edges, and posts in a database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.
Emit follow/block/post events to a message queue so downstream systems (notifications, feed pre-computation, analytics) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to follow so retried network requests cannot create duplicate follow attempts.
For high-follower accounts, precompute and cache feed results incrementally rather than recomputing on every read.
